title: DAP vs BIRP vs SOAP Notes in Behavioral Health: Examples That Hold Up in an Audit
summary: DAP, BIRP and SOAP notes organize the same progress note in different ways. See when each format fits, one fictional session written all three ways, and the elements every behavioral health note needs to hold up in a payer audit.
body_markdown:
DAP (Data, Assessment, Plan), BIRP (Behavior, Intervention, Response, Plan) and SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) are three ways to organize the same behavioral health progress note. None of the Medicare policies or state rules cited here requires one format, so pick the one that fits the service and use it consistently. Audits turn on content: time, modality, interventions tied to a plan goal, the client's response, progress, risk, next steps and a signature with credentials.


This guide is written for clinical directors and compliance leads who set the documentation standard for a whole team. It compares the formats, plus GIRP and PIE, shows when each fits, and writes one fictional session three ways. It also covers group notes, HIPAA psychotherapy notes, cloned documentation, timeliness and AI scribes. For the medical necessity chain behind every note, see our[medical necessity documentation guide](https://blog.adentris.com/medical-necessity-documentation-behavioral-health/) .


The short version


- No rule cited here requires DAP, BIRP or SOAP. Reviewers read content, not headings.
- Every note needs the same core: time, modality, participants, interventions tied to a named plan goal, response, progress, risk, next steps and a signature with credentials.
- Medicare LCD L33252 says statements such as "supportive psychotherapy given" are not adequate. Write what you did and how the client responded.
- Group notes need each member's own participation and response, not one paragraph pasted into every chart.
- Psychotherapy notes under 45 CFR 164.501 sit outside the progress note, and Medicare reviewers can't request them. Anything a payer needs belongs in the progress note.
- Cloned notes have their own CMS review finding. AI drafts are fine only when the clinician edits and signs them.


## DAP, BIRP and SOAP: how each format is built


All of these formats keep what you observed apart from what you concluded and what happens next. SOAP is the oldest. It comes from Lawrence Weed's problem-oriented medical record, set out in a 1968 New England Journal of Medicine article. DAP folds subjective and objective material into one Data section, and BIRP centers on behavior and what the clinician did.


Format Sections What goes where Usual fit


**SOAP** Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan S: the client's report. O: observable facts, mental status, scores. A: interpretation, progress, risk. P: next steps. Prescriber visits, nursing, integrated care


**DAP** Data, Assessment, Plan D: what the client reported, what you observed, the interventions used. A: interpretation and progress. P: homework and next session. Individual and family psychotherapy


**BIRP** Behavior, Intervention, Response, Plan B: presentation and behavior. I: what the clinician did. R: how the client responded. P: next steps. Groups, skills training, residential programming


**GIRP** Goal, Intervention, Response, Plan Opens with the plan goal addressed, then follows BIRP. Case management and community support


**PIE** Problem, Intervention, Evaluation A nursing format: the problem, the action, the result. Nursing in detox and residential units


The difference that matters in an audit is where the intervention goes. BIRP and GIRP give it a heading, so a gap is obvious. In DAP and SOAP it hides inside Data or Assessment, where lines like "processed feelings" creep in.


## When each format fits


Choose by service, not by clinician preference. Here's how we'd map it for a multi-service BH or SUD program:


- **Individual and family psychotherapy:** DAP, with a required interventions line.
- **Psychiatric and medication visits:** SOAP. Prescribers know it, and Objective is a natural home for vitals, labs and the mental status exam.
- **Groups, skills training and residential programming:** BIRP, because observed behavior and individual response are what a group note must show.
- **Case management and community support:** GIRP, which leads with the plan goal.
- **Nursing in withdrawal management:** PIE or SOAP, whichever your nurses already use for monitoring.


Our position: one format per service type across the organization. When every therapist writes in a personal format, nobody can scan the records quickly. Build templates so required fields can't be skipped, then let clinicians write freely inside them. If a state Medicaid manual, managed care contract or accreditor prescribes a structure, that wins.


## What every progress note needs, whatever the format


Medicare's psychotherapy policies describe content, not headings. First Coast's LCD L33252 wants each session's record to show symptoms "sufficient to alter baseline functioning," a detailed summary of the interventions, the degree of patient participation, and progress toward goals, including lack of change. Its billing article A57520 (revised October 1, 2026) adds legibility, a legible signature, and start and stop times or total time for 90832, 90834 and 90837.


CGS's LCD L34353 asks for the time spent, the therapeutic maneuvers used and a periodic summary of goals and progress. State rules echo this. Pennsylvania's Medical Assistance rule requires the record to "indicate the progress at each visit, change in diagnosis, change in treatment and response to treatment." For time thresholds by code, see our[psychotherapy CPT codes guide](https://blog.adentris.com/psychotherapy-cpt-codes-90832-90834-90837/) .


Element What to write Where the rule comes from


**Date** Full date of service, plus the signature date if different 55 Pa. Code 1101.51(e), WAC 246-341-0640


**Time** Start and stop times or total minutes A57520, L34353, WAC 246-341-0640


**Service type and modality** Individual, family or group. In person, video or audio-only, and client location for telehealth. Minn. Stat. 245G.06, subd. 2a (type of service)


**Participants** Who was present and their relationship to the client WAC 246-341-0640 (participant's name)


**Plan goal** The goal or objective addressed, in the plan's own words 14 NYCRR 599.11(b)(8), L34353


**Interventions** Named techniques and what you actually did L33252, Limitation 13


**Response** What the client said or did in response L33252, WAC 246-341-0640, Minn. Stat. 245G.06


**Progress** Change or no change since last session, with a measure where you have one L33252, 55 Pa. Code 1101.51(e)


**Risk** Current suicide, violence or relapse risk when indicated, and any action taken Clinical standard. None of these rules names it for every note.


**Plan** Next session, homework, referrals, and any plan change with the reason L33252, 55 Pa. Code 1101.51(e)


**Signature** Name, credential, signature and date A57520, WAC 246-341-0640, 55 Pa. Code 1101.51(e)


Two rows need a comment. Risk isn't a per-note element in these rules, but a note that ignores suicidal ideation charted the week before won't survive any review. And a note can only point to a goal the plan contains, which starts with the assessment. Our[biopsychosocial assessment guide](https://blog.adentris.com/biopsychosocial-assessment-behavioral-health-sud/) covers that step. New York's clinic rule puts the link plainly: progress notes must "relate to goals and objectives of treatment."


## One fictional session, written three ways


The samples below describe one invented session. Everything in them is fictional, and the notes are teaching examples, not clinical guidance.


- **Client:** "R.M.," 41, outpatient, alcohol use disorder, moderate, with depressive symptoms.
- **Session:** 11/05/2026, individual psychotherapy.
- **Plan dated 10/06/2026, Goal 2:** stay alcohol-free by managing high-risk situations. Objective 2a: name three triggers and rehearse a refusal plan for each by 11/30/2026.


Sample DAP note (fictional, for illustration only)


**Data.** Reports 21 days without alcohol since 10/15/2026. Cravings 6/10 this week, 8/10 at plan date. Says Friday's work happy hour is "the one I'm dreading." PHQ-9: 11 (15 at intake). Clinician did a functional analysis of the happy hour and led two role-plays of a refusal script with feedback. Denies suicidal ideation, intent or plan. C-SSRS screener negative.


**Assessment.** Progress on Goal 2, Objective 2a: two of three triggers named (work events, evenings alone). Needed two prompts in the first role-play, none in the second, so the skill is forming but not automatic. Relapse risk moderate around Friday. No current safety concerns.


**Plan.** Daily craving log. Text sponsor before and after Friday. Next session 11/12/2026 to identify the third trigger. PHQ-9 in two weeks. Treatment plan unchanged.


Individual psychotherapy, in person, client only, 10:02 to 10:47 (45 minutes). \[Clinician name\], LCSW. E-signed 11/05/2026 11:20.


Sample BIRP note (fictional, for illustration only)


**Behavior.** On time, anxious at first (fidgeting, rapid speech), engaged throughout. Reports 21 days without alcohol and cravings 6/10 (8/10 on 10/06/2026). Names Friday's happy hour as this week's highest-risk event. PHQ-9: 11. Denies suicidal ideation, intent or plan. C-SSRS screener negative.


**Intervention.** Targeted Goal 2, Objective 2a. Functional analysis of the happy hour, then two role-plays of a refusal script with feedback after each.


**Response.** Named a second trigger, evenings alone. Needed two prompts in the first role-play, none in the second. Said, "It's the second offer that gets me." Agreed to a craving log.


**Plan.** Craving log and sponsor contact before and after Friday. Next session 11/12/2026 for the third trigger. PHQ-9 in two weeks. Plan unchanged.


Sample SOAP note (fictional, for illustration only)


**Subjective.** "I'm dreading Friday." Reports 21 days without alcohol, cravings 6/10 (8/10 on 10/06/2026) and better sleep. Names evenings alone as a second trigger. Denies suicidal ideation, intent or plan.


**Objective.** In person, client only, 10:02 to 10:47 (45 minutes). Anxious affect early, brighter later. Thought process linear. PHQ-9: 11 (15 at intake). C-SSRS screener negative. Second refusal role-play done without prompting.


**Assessment.** Progress on Goal 2, Objective 2a. Interventions: functional analysis of the upcoming event, behavioral rehearsal with feedback. Skill forming, not automatic. Moderate relapse risk around Friday. No current safety concerns.


**Plan.** Daily craving log, sponsor contact around Friday. Next session 11/12/2026 for the third trigger. PHQ-9 in two weeks. Plan unchanged.


\[Clinician name\], LCSW. E-signed 11/05/2026 11:20.


Read them side by side. The headings are the only real difference. Each note names the goal, interventions, response, a measure of change, risk, the next step and the time, which is what an auditor scores.


## Weak vs strong: lines that fail review and lines that hold up


Element Weak Strong


**Time** "Session held." "10:02 to 10:47 (45 minutes)."


**Goal link** "Worked on treatment goals." "Goal 2, Objective 2a (plan dated 10/06/2026)."


**Interventions** "Supportive therapy provided." "Functional analysis of upcoming work event. Two refusal role-plays with feedback."


**Response** "Client receptive." "Needed two prompts in the first role-play, none in the second."


**Progress** "Progressing well." "Cravings 6/10, down from 8/10. PHQ-9 11, down from 15."


**Risk** Blank, or "N/A." "Denies suicidal ideation, intent or plan. C-SSRS screener negative."


**Plan** "Continue plan." "Daily craving log. Next session 11/12 for third trigger."


The weak column isn't a caricature. "Supportive therapy provided" is close to the very example L33252 calls inadequate.


### How a weak note becomes a denial


CMS's Generic Part B Reason Codes and Statements (June 9, 2025) show how Medicare reviewers word each gap:


Code CMS statement (short) Typical note gap behind it


**GBB02** Documentation incomplete and/or insufficient No time, intervention or response


**GBB11** Does not support the number of units billed Minutes don't support the units billed


**GBC02** Does not support medical necessity No symptoms, functional impact or progress


**GBD13** Contains cloned or altered information Copy-forward text, overwritten entries


**GBF01** No valid signature and/or credentials Unsigned note or missing credential


Free scorecard


SUD chart audit scorecard (Excel)


Score your own progress notes the way a payer reviewer would: 24 audit items across 10 charts, so you can see which elements your clinicians miss most before an audit finds them.

## Group notes


Group notes fail most often for one reason: the same paragraph pasted into every member's chart. A reviewer reading one client's record needs that client's participation and response.


Medicare adds limits. L33252 and L34353 both cap group psychotherapy at 12 participants, and L33252 requires the group to be ordered as part of an active treatment plan. L34353 excludes socialization, recreational activities, art classes, excursions and eating together, so a note describing an outing won't support a group psychotherapy claim.


A defensible group note has:


- The group name or type, date, start and stop times, and each facilitator's name and credential.
- The topic in one shared line, and the number attending.
- This member's participation and response, tied to their own plan goal.
- Any risk or behavior concern for this member, and what staff did.
- No other members' names. Write "a peer" instead.


That last point is risk control. When a chart goes to a payer or out under a Part 2 consent, every name inside it goes too. Washington's rule frames the test well: capture each person's "response to interventions or clinically significant behaviors during the group session."


## Psychotherapy notes vs progress notes under HIPAA


HIPAA defines psychotherapy notes narrowly. Under 45 CFR 164.501 they're a mental health professional's notes "documenting or analyzing the contents of conversation" in a counseling session, kept separate from the rest of the record. The definition excludes start and stop times, modalities and frequencies, test results, and any summary of diagnosis, functional status, treatment plan, symptoms, prognosis and progress. Everything an auditor needs is progress note material.


Psychotherapy notes Progress notes (DAP, BIRP, SOAP)


**Content** The clinician's analysis of what was said Time, modality, interventions, response, symptoms, progress, risk, plan


**Location** Separate from the medical record The medical record


**Disclosure** Authorization required for most uses (45 CFR 164.508(a)(2)) Usable for treatment, payment and operations, subject to Part 2 for SUD records


**Client access** Excluded from the right of access (45 CFR 164.524) Included


**Medicare review** Contractors may not request them (PIM Chapter 3, 3.3.2.6) What reviewers read


So if the progress note is thin and the substance sits in psychotherapy notes, the claim can't be defended. The Program Integrity Manual makes the provider responsible for extracting what supports the claim, and the claim is denied if that isn't enough. Merging both kinds of content into one document doesn't protect the progress-note material either.


SUD programs have a parallel category. The 2024 Part 2 final rule, with a compliance date of February 16, 2026, added "SUD counseling notes" to 42 CFR 2.11, with the same exclusions. Under 42 CFR 2.31(b), most uses and disclosures need a separate consent that can only be combined with another counseling-notes consent. See our[42 CFR Part 2 guide](https://blog.adentris.com/42-cfr-part-2-guide-2026/) for the rest.


## Cloned and copy-forward notes


A December 2015 CMS fact sheet on electronic health records describes cloning as copying and pasting information from a prior note into a new one. The record, it says, must show "the differences and the needs of the patient for each visit or encounter," and changing only the date isn't acceptable. A 2016 CMS fact sheet adds that HHS-OIG has named cloning and copy-and-paste among EHR features misused for fraud.


Behavioral health records clone easily. Weekly sessions, stable goals and a template full of smart phrases produce notes that read alike even when nobody pressed copy. CMS's reason list has its own statement for that (GBD13), and OIG's 2014 report recommended that CMS have its contractors use providers' audit logs. Plan as if a reviewer will ask for yours.


**Safe to carry forward, once reviewed:** demographics, diagnoses, the wording of plan goals, a medication list confirmed at the visit, and a re-reviewed safety plan.


**Write fresh every time:** what the client reported, observed presentation, this session's interventions, the client's response, progress or its absence, current risk, next steps and time.


Cloning is a pattern problem. It shows only when notes are compared across sessions and clinicians, which sampling rarely does. See our piece on[full-sweep chart audits versus sampling](https://blog.adentris.com/chart-audit-sud-full-sweep-vs-sampling/) .


## Timeliness, signatures and late entries


Medicare expects services "to be documented in the medical record at the time they are rendered" (PIM Chapter 3, section 3.3.2.5) but sets no universal deadline. States often do. Minnesota, for example, gives licensed SUD programs seven days to document each treatment service and the client's response.


When a note is late or wrong, add a dated, authored late entry or addendum. CMS wants the date and author of any amendment identifiable and the change clearly and permanently marked. Never change the date of service. Never overwrite the original.


Every note needs a signature with credentials, and a missing one has its own CMS finding (GBF01). For attestations, state deadlines and co-signature for pre-licensed clinicians, see our guide to[signature requirements for clinical notes](https://blog.adentris.com/signature-requirements-clinical-documentation/) .


## AI scribes and drafted notes


Nothing in the rules above forbids AI scribes or note-drafting tools. Nothing in them moves responsibility either. Medicare requires the person responsible for the care to be identifiable in the record, and the clinician who signs answers for every line, including lines a tool wrote.


Drafts carry specific risks. A model can describe an intervention that never happened. Weekly drafts can read alike, which is the cloning pattern above. And a raw transcript can hold the kind of conversation analysis HIPAA treats as psychotherapy notes, so decide by policy whether transcripts are kept.


States have started to regulate. Illinois's Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act, signed in August 2025, allows AI for administrative and supplementary support but bars it from therapeutic decision-making, with fines of up to $10,000, per the state's licensing agency. Other states are drafting similar bills, so check your state's rules before you switch a scribe on.


Before signing an AI draft, the clinician should:


1. Confirm every listed intervention actually happened.
2. Replace generic phrases with what this client said and did today.
3. Check the time against the session record, not the recording length.
4. Match the goal in the note to the current treatment plan.
5. Sign only after editing.


On the program side, get a business associate agreement with the vendor, plus a qualified service organization agreement for Part 2 records. For your AI policy, the September 2025 guidance from the Joint Commission and the Coalition for Health AI, built around policies, local validation and monitoring, is a sensible frame.

## Frequently asked questions


**What is the difference between DAP, BIRP and SOAP notes?**


They organize the same progress note under different headings. DAP uses Data, Assessment and Plan. BIRP uses Behavior, Intervention, Response and Plan. SOAP uses Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan. The content an auditor looks for is the same in all three.


**Does Medicare or Medicaid require a specific progress note format?**


None of the Medicare LCDs or state rules cited in this guide requires DAP, BIRP or SOAP. They specify content instead, such as time, interventions, response, progress and a signature. A Medicaid manual, managed care contract or accreditor can still require a structure.


**What must every behavioral health progress note include?**


The date, start and stop times or total time, service type and modality, who was present, the plan goal addressed, specific interventions, the client's response, progress, current risk when indicated, next steps, and the clinician's signature with credentials and date.


**Are psychotherapy notes the same as progress notes?**


No. Under 45 CFR 164.501, psychotherapy notes analyze the contents of a counseling session and are kept separate from the medical record. Times, modality, symptoms, the treatment plan and progress belong in the progress note. Medicare review contractors may not request psychotherapy notes.


**Is it okay to copy forward parts of a previous note?**


Stable facts such as demographics, diagnoses and the wording of plan goals can carry forward once reviewed. Session content, response, progress, risk and the plan must be new each time. Medicare reviewers have a specific finding for cloned documentation.


**Can an AI scribe write my progress notes?**


An AI tool can draft a note, but the clinician must review and sign it and is responsible for its content. Check that every listed intervention happened, the time matches the session and the goal matches the current plan. Some states, including Illinois, now regulate AI use in therapy.
